newsitem.title: USA: New chief US spymaster has golden credentials.
newsitem.headline: New chief US spymaster has golden credentials.

text.p: George Tenet, confirmed by the Senate on Thursday as the new director of central intelligence, has risen smoothly through staff ranks in Congress and the White House to become the nation's chief spymaster.

Tenet, praised by lawmakers for his professionalism, character and judgment, once served as staff director of the Senate Intelligence Committee, which unanimously approved his nomination earlier Thursday.

He will be President Bill Clinton's third CIA director after John Deutch, who left in December after 20 months in the job, and James Woolsey, who quit in December 1994 after becoming entangled in the case of convicted CIA turncoat Aldrich Ames.
Tenet took over as deputy director of intelligence in July 1995 and has been acting CIA director since December.
"I have confidence in him and I am confident that he will represent our country very well in this important post," said Sen. John Warner, a Virginia Republican.

Clinton's first choice for the spymaster job, former national security adviser Anthony Lake, withdrew his name from consideration in March and condemned the confirmation process as "nasty and brutish without being short."

Tenet's nomination initially seemed likely to sail through the Senate intelligence panel, but hit a snag when the Justice Department began investigating his failure to disclose a part interest in stocks and real estate inherited from his father.

The Justice Department on Wednesday removed that hurdle and paved the way for the Senate vote when it ended a preliminary investigation into the matter and saw no need to appoint an independent counsel.
In a statement issued moments after the Senate vote, Tenet pledged to provide the president and others with "intelligence that is clear, objective and does not pull punches."
To lawmakers, he said, "You can expect forthright and candid views about our missions, programmes, and priorities, I will not hold back."
Tenet, 44, worked at the White House from 1993 until 1995 as chief intelligence adviser to Lake.

He coordinated all U.S. covert actions abroad while at the National Security Council, and crafted presidential directives on intelligence priorities, security coordination, spy-catching and satellite remote-sensing policies.

A sometimes gruff cigar-smoker said by colleagues to have a keen sense of humour, Tenet's Capitol Hill experience came as staff director on the Senate Intelligence Committee from 1988-93 under then-Chairman David Boren, an Oklahoma Democrat.

In that job Tenet pushed for tightened rules on the reporting of U.S. covert actions to Congress's intelligence panels in light of the 1986-87 Iran-Contra affair, President Ronald Reagan's worst foreign policy fiasco in which White House aides secretly sold arms to Tehran and diverted profits to Nicaragua's contra rebels.
In his confirmation hearings in May, Tenet warned about the risk of "fanatical terrorists" that he said stepped up their capabilities worldwide to move money and people and explosives.
In his statement, Tenet said he planned on "closing the door on the Cold War" to focus more sharply on transnational threats such as narcotics traffickers, nuclear proliferation and terrorism.
As director of central intelligence, Tenet will run the CIA and also oversee 12 other U.S. spy agencies that employ tens of thousands of people and spend about $30 billion a year overall.
Associates said Tenet would be a popular choice with the CIA covert operations directorate, tarnished and shaken by the spy scandals. He has worked with the covert operations directorate for years.

George J. Tenet was born Jan. 5, 1953, in New York. He received a bachelor's degree from Georgetown University School of Foreign Service in 1976 and a master's from Columbia University School of International Affairs in 1978.
The son of a Greek immigrant father and mother who fled Albania, Tenet grew up in the New York City borough of Queens, where he once cleaned tables at his parents' diner.
A resident of Potomac, Maryland, he is married to A. Stephanie Glakas-Tenet. They have one son, John Michael.
